Data wrangling

Reading and wrangling data with the {tidyverse}

Dr Massimiliano Canzi

Today

By the end of this class you will be able to

  • recognise tidy data, and turn wide data into long data
  • read and write .csv files with {readr}
  • use the core {dplyr} verbs select(), filter(), arrange(), rename() and mutate(), and summarise data by group with summarise() and count()
  • chain everything together with the pipe |>

The tidyverse

“R is not a language driven by the purity of its philosophy; R is a language designed to get shit done.”

Hadley Wickham (Chief Scientist at Posit, formerly RStudio)

Tidyverse

In lecture 1 we called the tidyverse a dialect of R. Its packages share the same design, grammar and data structures, and everything you know from base R still works.

  • Functions are verbs, named after what they do
  • The data always comes first, so functions can be chained
  • Output is (almost) always a data frame, which tells the next step what to expect
  • With Quarto or R Markdown, the whole analysis becomes reproducible

Base R vs tidyverse

Same question: mean body mass of Gentoo penguins, in kg

Base R

gentoo <- penguins[penguins$species == "Gentoo", ]
mean(gentoo$body_mass_g / 1000, na.rm = TRUE)

tidyverse

penguins |>
  filter(species == "Gentoo") |>
  summarise(mass_kg = mean(body_mass_g / 1000,
                           na.rm = TRUE))

Both give the same answer; the tidyverse version reads more like a sentence.

The core tidyverse

library(tidyverse) loads nine packages:

Package What it does
readr read and write rectangular data (.csv, .tsv)
tibble a modern data frame
dplyr manipulate data: filter, select, mutate, summarise
tidyr reshape data (wide to long and back)
ggplot2 plots
stringr work with text
forcats work with factors (categorical variables)
lubridate work with dates and times
purrr apply functions repeatedly (iteration)

The typical workflow

Almost every analysis goes through the same steps, and each has its own tools:

Import Tidy Transform Visualise Model Communicate
{readr} {tidyr} {dplyr} {ggplot2} lm() and friends Quarto, R Markdown
today today today next class lectures 4–13 your assignment

The steps are not a straight line: plotting often sends you back to transform, and a model often sends you back to plot.

Tidy data

A data set is tidy when

  1. each variable is a column
  2. each observation is a row
  3. each value is a cell

Frequency is a variable. Where is it?

Untidy (wide)

participant rt_high rt_low
P01 580 642
P02 611 690

Tidy (long)

participant frequency rt
P01 high 580
P01 low 642
P02 high 611
P02 low 690

Discussion

You record 20 speakers reading the same 30 words, and measure F1, F2 and the duration of each vowel.

  • What is one row in your tidy data set? Which columns do you need?
  • Where would information about the speakers, such as age or dialect, go?

From wide to long

pivot_longer() from {tidyr} turns the wide table into a tidy one:

wide <- tibble(participant = c("P01", "P02"), rt_high = c(580, 611), rt_low = c(642, 690))
wide |>
  pivot_longer(c(rt_high, rt_low), names_to = "frequency", values_to = "rt",
               names_prefix = "rt_")
# A tibble: 4 × 3
  participant frequency    rt
  <chr>       <chr>     <dbl>
1 P01         high        580
2 P01         low         642
3 P02         high        611
# ℹ 1 more row

pivot_wider() goes the other way, which is sometimes handy for tables in a paper.

Tibbles

A tibble is a data frame with nicer defaults.

penguins
# A tibble: 344 × 8
  species island    bill_length_mm bill_depth_mm flipper_length_mm
  <fct>   <fct>              <dbl>         <dbl>             <int>
1 Adelie  Torgersen           39.1          18.7               181
2 Adelie  Torgersen           39.5          17.4               186
3 Adelie  Torgersen           40.3          18                 195
# ℹ 341 more rows
# ℹ 3 more variables: body_mass_g <int>, sex <fct>, year <int>

It prints only the first rows and the columns that fit, and shows the type of each column: <fct>, <dbl>, <int>, <chr>.

glimpse()

A transposed overview: one line per column.

glimpse(penguins)
Rows: 344
Columns: 8
$ species           <fct> Adelie, Adelie, Adelie, Adelie, Adelie, Ad…
$ island            <fct> Torgersen, Torgersen, Torgersen, Torgersen…
$ bill_length_mm    <dbl> 39.1, 39.5, 40.3, NA, 36.7, 39.3, 38.9, 39…
$ bill_depth_mm     <dbl> 18.7, 17.4, 18.0, NA, 19.3, 20.6, 17.8, 19…
$ flipper_length_mm <int> 181, 186, 195, NA, 193, 190, 181, 195, 193…
$ body_mass_g       <int> 3750, 3800, 3250, NA, 3450, 3650, 3625, 46…
$ sex               <fct> male, female, female, NA, female, male, fe…
$ year              <int> 2007, 2007, 2007, 2007, 2007, 2007, 2007, …

Example data

Did you know: the 344 rows of the penguins data are real birds: adult Adélie, Chinstrap and Gentoo penguins nesting near Palmer Station, Antarctica, measured by Dr Kristen Gorman and the Palmer Station LTER team from 2007 to 2009.

Sources: Gorman, Williams & Fraser (2014), PLoS ONE; palmerpenguins documentation

The penguins data

344 penguins of 3 species, from 3 islands in the Palmer Archipelago (Antarctica). The data come with {konstats}, in the package {palmerpenguins}:

library(palmerpenguins)

Two penguins data sets

Heads up! Since R 4.5.0, base R also ships a penguins data set, but with shorter column names:

{palmerpenguins} base R ≥ 4.5.0
bill_length_mm bill_len
bill_depth_mm bill_dep
flipper_length_mm flipper_len
body_mass_g body_mass

In this course we always load {palmerpenguins} first. If you get object 'bill_length_mm' not found, you forgot!

{readr}

Reading and writing files

Function For files that look like
read_csv() word,rt with commas between values
read_tsv() values separated by tabs
read_csv2() word;rt with semicolons and decimal commas, as in German Excel exports
read_delim() any other separator
write_csv() saves a data frame as a .csv file 
library(readr)
data <- read_csv("data/my_file.csv")
write_csv(data, "data/my_file_clean.csv")

What read_csv() tells you

rt <- read_csv(example_file)
Rows: 6 Columns: 5
── Column specification ──────────────────────────────────────────────
Delimiter: ","
chr (3): participant, word, frequency
dbl (2): rt, accuracy

ℹ Use `spec()` to retrieve the full column specification for this data.
ℹ Specify the column types or set `show_col_types = FALSE` to quiet this message.
  • How many rows and columns it read, and the type it guessed for each column
  • If a guess is wrong, you can set the type yourself:
rt <- read_csv("data/rt.csv",
               col_types = cols(participant = col_factor()))

read_csv() vs read.csv()

read_csv() read.csv()
Package {readr} base R
Returns tibble data.frame
Speed fast slower on large files
Reports column types yes no

Use read_csv() (with an _) in this course.

{dplyr}

Did you know: Adélie penguins take their name from Adélie Land in Antarctica, which the French explorer Jules Dumont d’Urville named after his wife, Adèle, in 1840.

Source: Australian Antarctic Division

The grammar of {dplyr}

Every {dplyr} verb works the same way:

  1. The first argument is a data frame
  2. The other arguments say what to do, using column names without quotes
  3. The output is a new data frame

Six verbs

Verb Works on Does
select() columns keep or drop columns
rename() columns change column names
mutate() columns create or change columns
filter() rows keep rows that match a condition
arrange() rows sort rows
summarise() groups collapse many rows into one

The verb never changes your data

filter(penguins, species == "Gentoo")
# A tibble: 124 × 8
  species island bill_length_mm bill_depth_mm flipper_length_mm
  <fct>   <fct>           <dbl>         <dbl>             <int>
1 Gentoo  Biscoe           46.1          13.2               211
2 Gentoo  Biscoe           50            16.3               230
3 Gentoo  Biscoe           48.7          14.1               210
# ℹ 121 more rows
# ℹ 3 more variables: body_mass_g <int>, sex <fct>, year <int>
nrow(penguins)
[1] 344

penguins still has all its rows. To keep the result, assign it:

gentoo <- filter(penguins, species == "Gentoo")
nrow(gentoo)
[1] 124

Columns

select()

Keep the columns you name:

select(penguins, species, bill_length_mm)
# A tibble: 344 × 2
  species bill_length_mm
  <fct>            <dbl>
1 Adelie            39.1
2 Adelie            39.5
3 Adelie            40.3
# ℹ 341 more rows

Drop a column with -

select(penguins, -year)

select() helpers

Select by name pattern or type instead of typing every name:

In select(penguins, ...) Selects
species:bill_depth_mm a range of columns
starts_with("bill") names starting with “bill”
ends_with("_mm") names ending with “_mm”
contains("length") names containing “length”
where(is.numeric) all numeric columns
sex, everything() all columns, with sex moved to the front 
select(penguins, ends_with("_mm"))
# A tibble: 344 × 3
  bill_length_mm bill_depth_mm flipper_length_mm
           <dbl>         <dbl>             <int>
1           39.1          18.7               181
2           39.5          17.4               186
3           40.3          18                 195
# ℹ 341 more rows

select() by position

Also possible, but fragile:

select(penguins, 1, 3, 5)
select(penguins, 1:4)
select(penguins, -(1:5))

If the column order changes, for example in a new data export or a colleague’s file, your code silently selects the wrong columns. Selecting by name avoids this.

rename()

new_name = old_name

rename(penguins, Type = species)
# A tibble: 344 × 8
  Type   island    bill_length_mm bill_depth_mm flipper_length_mm
  <fct>  <fct>              <dbl>         <dbl>             <int>
1 Adelie Torgersen           39.1          18.7               181
2 Adelie Torgersen           39.5          17.4               186
3 Adelie Torgersen           40.3          18                 195
# ℹ 341 more rows
# ℹ 3 more variables: body_mass_g <int>, sex <fct>, year <int>

select() can rename too, but drops everything you do not name:

select(penguins, Type = species, bill_length_mm)
# A tibble: 344 × 2
  Type   bill_length_mm
  <fct>           <dbl>
1 Adelie           39.1
2 Adelie           39.5
3 Adelie           40.3
# ℹ 341 more rows

mutate()

Create new columns, or overwrite existing ones:

penguins_2 <- mutate(penguins,
                     body_mass_kg = body_mass_g / 1000,
                     bill_ratio = bill_length_mm / bill_depth_mm)
select(penguins_2, species, body_mass_kg, bill_ratio)
# A tibble: 344 × 3
  species body_mass_kg bill_ratio
  <fct>          <dbl>      <dbl>
1 Adelie          3.75       2.09
2 Adelie          3.8        2.27
3 Adelie          3.25       2.24
# ℹ 341 more rows

New columns are added at the end. You can use a column you just created in the same mutate().

mutate() with conditions

if_else() for two outcomes

mutate(penguins, size = if_else(body_mass_g > 4500, "large", "small"))

case_when() for more than two. Conditions are checked in order, and rows matching none of them get NA:

penguins_2 <- mutate(penguins,
  size = case_when(
    body_mass_g < 3500 ~ "small",
    body_mass_g < 4500 ~ "medium",
    body_mass_g >= 4500 ~ "large"
  )
)
count(penguins_2, size)
# A tibble: 4 × 2
  size       n
  <chr>  <int>
1 large    118
2 medium   153
3 small     71
# ℹ 1 more row

mutate() on many columns: across()

mutate_if() and mutate_all() are superseded: they still work, but are no longer developed. Use across():

mutate_if(penguins, is.factor, as.character)

is now written as:

mutate(penguins, across(where(is.factor), as.character))

across(columns, function): apply this function to these columns

mutate(penguins, across(ends_with("_mm"), \(x) x / 10))

\(x) x / 10 is a short way to write a small function: take x, divide it by 10. Here it turns millimetres into centimetres.

Rows

filter()

Keep the rows where a condition is TRUE:

filter(penguins, species == "Gentoo")
# A tibble: 124 × 8
  species island bill_length_mm bill_depth_mm flipper_length_mm
  <fct>   <fct>           <dbl>         <dbl>             <int>
1 Gentoo  Biscoe           46.1          13.2               211
2 Gentoo  Biscoe           50            16.3               230
3 Gentoo  Biscoe           48.7          14.1               210
# ℹ 121 more rows
# ℹ 3 more variables: body_mass_g <int>, sex <fct>, year <int>

Comparison operators

Operator Meaning Example
== equal to species == "Gentoo"
!= not equal to species != "Gentoo"
>, >= greater than (or equal) body_mass_g > 4000
<, <= less than (or equal) year <= 2008
%in% one of island %in% c("Biscoe", "Dream")
is.na() missing is.na(sex)

= assigns, == compares. filter(penguins, species = "Gentoo") gives an error.

Combining conditions

, or &: both must be true (AND)

filter(penguins, species == "Gentoo", body_mass_g > 5000)
filter(penguins, species == "Gentoo" & body_mass_g > 5000)

|: at least one must be true (OR)

filter(penguins, species == "Gentoo" | species == "Chinstrap")

%in% is shorter when matching several values of one column

unique(filter(penguins, species %in% c("Gentoo", "Chinstrap"))$species)
[1] Gentoo    Chinstrap
Levels: Adelie Chinstrap Gentoo

filter() and missing values

filter() drops rows where the condition is NA.

nrow(penguins)
[1] 344
sum(is.na(penguins$sex))
[1] 11
nrow(filter(penguins, sex == "female"))
[1] 165
nrow(filter(penguins, sex != "female"))
[1] 168

165 + 168 is 333, and penguins has 344 rows. Both filters drop the 11 penguins whose sex is unknown.

Discussion

In a listening experiment, some participants did not respond on a few trials, so those cells are NA.

  • Should these trials be removed, kept as NA, or counted as wrong answers?
  • Does your answer depend on why the response is missing?

filter_out() (new in {dplyr} 1.2.0)

Say which rows to drop. Rows with NA are kept.

nrow(filter_out(penguins, sex == "female"))
[1] 179

Rule of thumb:

  • filter() when you know what to keep
  • filter_out() when you know what to drop

Requires {dplyr} ≥ 1.2.0. Check with packageVersion("dplyr").

arrange()

Sort rows, smallest first

arrange(penguins, body_mass_g)
# A tibble: 344 × 8
  species   island bill_length_mm bill_depth_mm flipper_length_mm
  <fct>     <fct>           <dbl>         <dbl>             <int>
1 Chinstrap Dream            46.9          16.6               192
2 Adelie    Biscoe           36.5          16.6               181
3 Adelie    Biscoe           36.4          17.1               184
# ℹ 341 more rows
# ℹ 3 more variables: body_mass_g <int>, sex <fct>, year <int>

Largest first with desc(); sort by several columns in turn

arrange(penguins, desc(body_mass_g))
arrange(penguins, species, desc(body_mass_g))

Groups

Did you know: chinstrap penguins sleep in microsleeps: more than 10,000 a day, about 4 seconds each, which add up to about 11 hours of sleep.

Source: Libourel et al. (2023), Science

summarise()

Collapse many rows into one

summarise(penguins,
          mean_mass = mean(body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE),
          sd_mass = sd(body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE),
          n = n())
# A tibble: 1 × 3
  mean_mass sd_mass     n
      <dbl>   <dbl> <int>
1     4202.    802.   344

na.rm = TRUE ignores missing values. Without it, one NA makes the whole result NA.

group_by() + summarise()

One row per group

penguins_grouped <- group_by(penguins, species)
summarise(penguins_grouped,
          mean_mass = mean(body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE),
          n = n())
# A tibble: 3 × 3
  species   mean_mass     n
  <fct>         <dbl> <int>
1 Adelie        3701.   152
2 Chinstrap     3733.    68
3 Gentoo        5076.   124

group_by() changes nothing you can see. It tells the next verb to work group by group.

.by: grouping for one step

Same result, without a separate group_by():

summarise(penguins,
          mean_mass = mean(body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE),
          n = n(),
          .by = c(species, sex))
# A tibble: 8 × 4
  species sex    mean_mass     n
  <fct>   <fct>      <dbl> <int>
1 Adelie  male       4043.    73
2 Adelie  female     3369.    73
3 Adelie  <NA>       3540      6
# ℹ 5 more rows

.by groups for this verb only, so you never forget to ungroup(). It works in summarise(), mutate(), filter() and slice().

count()

A shortcut for counting rows per group

count(penguins, species, island)
# A tibble: 5 × 3
  species island        n
  <fct>   <fct>     <int>
1 Adelie  Biscoe       44
2 Adelie  Dream        56
3 Adelie  Torgersen    52
# ℹ 2 more rows

Same counts as summarise(penguins, n = n(), .by = c(species, island)), but count() also sorts the rows by group.

The pipe

Did you know: gentoo penguins are the fastest swimming birds: they reach about 36 km/h in short bursts, close to Usain Bolt’s average speed in his 100 m world record.

Source: Guinness World Records

Without the pipe

Three steps, three intermediate objects:

penguins_2 <- filter(penguins, species == "Gentoo" | species == "Chinstrap")
penguins_3 <- mutate(penguins_2, bill_length_cm = bill_length_mm / 10)
penguins_4 <- select(penguins_3, species, bill_length_cm)

Or nested, read from the inside out:

penguins_4 <- select(
  mutate(
    filter(penguins, species == "Gentoo" | species == "Chinstrap"),
    bill_length_cm = bill_length_mm / 10),
  species, bill_length_cm)

The pipe |>

x |> f(y) is the same as f(x, y)

  • The pipe takes the result on the left and passes it as the first argument of the function on the right
  • Read it aloud as “then”, so you do not repeat the object at every step
penguins_2 <- penguins |>
  filter(species == "Gentoo" | species == "Chinstrap") |>
  mutate(bill_length_cm = bill_length_mm / 10) |>
  select(species, bill_length_cm)
penguins_2
# A tibble: 192 × 2
  species bill_length_cm
  <fct>            <dbl>
1 Gentoo            4.61
2 Gentoo            5   
3 Gentoo            4.87
# ℹ 189 more rows

Reading a pipe aloud

Code Read it as
penguins_2 <- penguins |> Take penguins, then
filter(species == "Gentoo" | species == "Chinstrap") |> keep only Gentoo and Chinstrap penguins, then
mutate(bill_length_cm = bill_length_mm / 10) |> add bill length in cm, then
select(species, bill_length_cm) keep only these two columns.

Store the result as penguins_2. A pipe that you cannot read aloud like this is probably doing too much at once.

PRO TIP! Save to the right

penguins |>
  filter(species == "Gentoo" | species == "Chinstrap") |>
  mutate(bill_length_cm = bill_length_mm / 10) |>
  select(species, bill_length_cm) -> penguins_2

Same output as the previous slide. The code now reads top to bottom in the order things happen.

|> vs %>%

You will see two pipes in the wild:

  • %>% comes from {magrittr} and is loaded with the tidyverse (since 2014)
  • |> is built into R itself, since R 4.1.0

For everything in this course they are interchangeable. We use |>: it works without loading any package.

Keyboard shortcut: Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + M

To make it insert |>: Tools > Global Options > Code > Use native pipe operator

From wrangling to plotting

The output of a pipe can go straight into {ggplot2}

penguins |>
  filter_out(is.na(sex)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g, colour = species)) +
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.8) +
  labs(x = "Flipper length (mm)", y = "Body mass (g)", colour = NULL)

Note: {ggplot2} layers are added with +, not |>. More next class.

From wrangling to plotting

Common errors

Common errors

You wrote Problem
filter(df, species = "Gentoo") = instead of ==
filter(df, species == Gentoo) text values need "quotes"
select(df, Species) names are case sensitive
filter(df, ...) and nothing changes result not assigned with <-
mean(body_mass_g) gives NA missing values: add na.rm = TRUE
object 'bill_length_mm' not found forgot library(palmerpenguins)
could not find function "filter_out" {dplyr} older than 1.2.0

Summary

  • {readr}: read_csv(), write_csv()
  • Columns: select(), rename(), mutate(), across()
  • Rows: filter(), filter_out(), arrange()
  • Groups: summarise(), count(), group_by() or .by
  • Chain with |>, read as “then”
  • Always assign the result if you want to keep it
